transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-13
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Emily Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Aurelia CTO), Liam Rivera (Aurelia ML), Priya Nair (Aurelia PM)
Links shared: deck: https://redwood.app/decks/aurelia-demo , security packet: https://redwood.app/security/aurelia (placeholder)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be brief):
- Intro to Redwood hosted API for chat and text generation.
- Live sandbox demo showing streaming tokens, param tuning (temp/top_p/max_tokens), and retry/backoff patterns.
- Discussed security posture (SOC 2, SSO/SAML, KMS) and data residency concerns.
- Agreed to run a benchmark pilot and share security docs + pricing.

Topics covered:
- Streaming vs sync calls, when to use each
- Parameter effects: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop tokens, logit_bias
- Idempotency and retries, exponential backoff, idempotency keys for non-streaming flows
- Console sandbox for token/latency cost visibility and Optimize suggestions

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Samir from Redwood, and with me is Emily, our SE. Quick intro?
[00:07] Maya: Hi, Maya here — quick context, we're building a patient triage chat for our telehealth flow; latency SLOs are pretty strict and we're worried about token costs.
[00:15] Emily: Awesome. We'll show the hosted API flow and the sandbox console — also cover retries and parameter knobs. Quick question — what's your expected peak qps?
[00:24] Liam: Peak is around 120 requests per minute in the worst window, but bursts up to ~400 for marketing events. Mostly short dialogs, avg 30 tokens per response.
[00:34] Samir: Good to know. Hosted generally works well for that profile; we can also recommend dedicated if you want hard throughput SLOs. But let's jump into the sandbox.
[01:05] Emily: (shares screen) This is the Playground — quick note, transcription sometimes calls it the "playground" or "play play"... but you get the idea. I'll send link.
[01:20] Emily: We're sending a streaming chat request here — you can see tokens arrive chunked. For streams, you get lower perceived latency cause partial tokens show up earlier.
[01:35] Priya: What does that look like for error handling? If the stream dies midway, do we get partials and then retry?
[01:43] Emily: Good question. There are two patterns. For streaming clients, we typically surface partials to the user and then re-request missing content via a non-streaming retry using an idempotency key, or we fall back to a shorter-safe model variant. You have to design de-dup logic client-side a little.
[02:05] Maya: So idempotency keys only for non-streaming?
[02:09] Emily: Right, streaming is ephemeral — but you can track a per-message id and reconcile. For guaranteed exactly-once full responses you do sync call + idempotency keys and backoff.
[02:25] Samir: Also keep in mind our platform has automatic prefix caching and kv cache. That helps repeated prompts, so follow-ups are cheaper. Sometimes the transcript says K-V cache as "K V" which is fun in captions.
[02:40] Liam: How do we tune temperature and top_p for clinical text vs more conversational triage? We need conservative outputs.
[02:48] Emily: Lower temperature, maybe 0.0–0.2, top_p 0.8–0.95 depending on fuzziness. Also use system-level prompt to constrain style. And always include stop tokens for safety.
[03:05] Priya: Any native guardrails? Like hallucination checks?
[03:08] Emily: We surface quality monitors and can do regression alerts based on your eval prompts. Redwood Optimize will suggest quantization and model variant tradeoffs as well.
[03:20] (small cross-talk)
[03:40] [Demo step — live request]
[03:41] Emily: Sending a sample patient message — watch the stream.
[03:50] [streaming tokens appear in console]
[04:10] Maya: Looks snappy. Latency seems ~120ms per chunk here?
[04:14] Emily: The console shows token timing and per-route breakdown. This specific model is tuned for low-latency small responses.
[04:32] Liam: What about retry budgets? If we get transient 503s, what's recommended?
[04:36] Samir: We recommend exponential backoff with jitter, cap at 3 attempts for user-facing low-latency calls. For background jobs you can increase. Also configure circuit-breaker in front of the API.
[04:52] Emily: And for idempotency keys: if you attach one to a generation call, the platform will dedupe duplicate requests for sync calls. For stream, tie a client message id and reconcile.
[05:10] Priya: Does Redwood store prompt/response pairs? Concerned about PHI.
[05:16] Samir: By default hosted API stores data for 30 days for diagnostics, but for regulated data we offer Private deployments or can opt out of retention — we also have a Dedicated/Private option where logs aren't retained. We'll share the SOC 2 / data retention section in that packet.
[05:35] Maya: We need KMS integration — customer-managed keys.
[05:39] Samir: Yes, KMS/HSM integrations available for Private and Dedicated. Hosted can also integrate with cloud KMS in enterprise plans. We'll include specifics.
[05:55] Liam: How do you route requests regionally? We need EU residency for some workflows.
[06:01] Emily: You can pin routes to regions; the smart router sends by policy. For EU residency we can host within the EU region or deploy Private in your VPC.
[06:18] Maya: Back to parameters — how do you recommend handling stop tokens versus truncating?
[06:23] Emily: Stop tokens are best to avoid partial trailing text. Truncation is a last resort; it's better to include explicit stops.
[06:35] Priya: Can we do streaming for long surveys?
[06:38] Emily: For long outputs streaming helps perceived latency, but network stability matters. For very long sequences we also recommend chunking responses and resumable flows.
[07:05] [15-minute mark — demo continues with console metrics]
[15:02] Emily: Here's the Console Optimize tab — it suggests batching and model quantization recommendations for your workload. For short 30-token responses batching isn't as beneficial, but prefix caching helps a lot.
[15:25] Liam: You mentioned automatic batching in the runtime — how does that affect latency variability?
[15:30] Emily: We have continuous batching — it waits up to a configured window to batch requests, but for low-latency routes you can set batch window to near-zero. There is a tradeoff: more batching = lower cost per token, slightly higher tail latency.
[15:48] Maya: Any SLA on latency for hosted?
[15:50] Samir: Hosted has best-effort latency targets in the docs; Dedicated offers SLA-backed latency tiers. We'll outline options in the pricing packet.
[16:05] Priya: If we need to fall back to a smaller model during congestion, is that automatic?
[16:09] Emily: You can configure fallback policies — e.g., if model variant A is overloaded, route to B which is cheaper. Redwood supports automated fallback and rollbacks. Sometimes captions say "rollout policy" as "roll out police" — transcription quirk.
[16:25] Liam: For benchmarking, what metrics should we collect?
[16:28] Emily: Latency p50/p95/p99, per-token cost, success rate (no errors), and quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE or human evals depending). We'll share a template.
[16:45] [Long pause — demo walkthrough of failure modes]
[22:30] Emily: Now I'll intentionally cause a transient 502 to show retry behavior.
[22:35] [console shows 502, then backoff and successful retry]
[22:47] Priya: Good example. We liked that the client showed partials and then patched them.
[23:10] Samir: For clients, best practice is show partials with a spinner and then merge with final response. If duplicate content occurs, reconcile with the message id.
[23:33] Maya: On compliance — any third-party audits?
[23:36] Samir: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 in progress; security packet has attestation list. We'll send it.
[24:00] Liam: Are there libraries for idempotency and streaming helpers?
[24:03] Emily: Yes — our SDKs (Python/JS) include streaming helpers, idempotency helpers, and examples for retries/backoff. Some of the transcription spells SDKs as "S-D-K's," just FYI.
[24:20] Priya: What's the integration effort? We have mobile + web clients.
[24:24] Samir: For mobile/web mostly simple REST/Websocket streaming integration. We'll share a quickstart that gets you to a sandbox in under a day.
[24:40] Maya: About costs — can we get sample per-token math for our expected volume?
[24:44] Samir: Yes, I'll attach a sample pricing sheet with modeled monthly costs at 120 rps and at 400 burst. It'll show per-token and estimated monthly spend.
[25:10] Emily: Also show how Optimize suggests quantizing a model for lower cost; note that sometimes quantization impacts output quality slightly — we'll show tradeoff graphs.
[25:35] [Customer asks about running local benchmarks]
[25:37] Liam: If we run an internal benchmark using our dataset, can Redwood run a head-to-head?
[25:42] Samir: Absolutely — Emily will coordinate. For hosted we'd run a controlled benchmark; if you want fully private data we can do Dedicated or Private runs.
[26:05] Priya: Next steps?
[26:07] Samir: I'll send security + pricing. Emily to propose a benchmark plan. You to share prompts and traffic profile.
[26:15] Maya: Sounds good.
[26:20] [Wrap-up conversation — light banter]
[26:55] Priya: One more quick question — how do you support SSO for multiple product teams?
[27:00] Samir: SAML/SSO and RBAC are supported in enterprise plans; we can scope roles and audit logging.
[27:10] Maya: Ok let's lock in the technical deep dive next week.
[27:15] Emily: I'll send invites for 2 hours slots next Tue/Thu.
[27:27] [Silence, meeting ends]

Recap (auto):
- Demo of hosted chat streaming, parameter tuning, and retry patterns.
- Discussed data retention, KMS, SSO, and EU residency.
- Agreed to share SOC2/security packet, pricing, and run a benchmark pilot.

Notes on transcription quirks: names misheard at times (e.g., "Aurelia" became "Auralia" in parts), product terms like "KV cache" as "K V cache", and "rollout" as "rollout police" in a couple spots.

End of transcript.
